name: Elena Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up for an eight o'clock lecture most days, computer science, so programming and a maths-for-computing module that I'm enjoying more than I expected. I live in a shared flat with two girls from my course. On Friday nights and all day Sunday I go back to my parents' restaurant, where I do the till and, increasingly, the bookkeeping, because I'm good with spreadsheets. My parents bought the restaurant eleven years ago, and my little brother Kenta is twelve and does his homework at table six. I go to the temple with my grandmother when I'm home, and I think that part of my life keeps me steady. I use an AI tool for explaining code sometimes, but I'm cautious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reassuring, and a bit unexciting. At the restaurant I'd say, good, then nothing changes for us, and we can focus on food. To my course mates I'd say it's another bubble, like others before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about my degree, but not about the restaurant. Rents and ingredients keep rising, and my parents work six days a week. A plateau doesn't fix that. I carry that worry all the time, because if the restaurant fails, there's no plan B for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue as normal: study hard, work at the restaurant, and help with the books. I'd try to build a simple spreadsheet that shows my parents which dishes make money and which don't. And I'd ask the department about a summer placement, even a small one, so I can add something real to my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about me, tight about the family. A bit like carrying a full bowl of soup across a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which dishes lose money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet, which is why I'd build it. My guess is the sashimi plate, because fish prices jump. Dad loves it, though, so I'd have to show him kindly. He's proud of it, and I'd never want to embarrass him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your parents listen to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd listen, slowly. In our house, respect goes up the family, not down. Still, numbers on a page are hard to argue with. Mum is practical, so I'd start with her.

To course mates I'd say it's **another bubble**.

If the restaurant fails, there is **no plan B** for the family.

Keep working at the **restaurant** and doing the books.
Ask the department about a **summer placement**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that this is a chance for small businesses to use tools big firms already have, so don't be afraid of it. To my friends I'd say learn the tools and still do the basic work yourself. At the temple, I'd say nothing, because it's not a topic for there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel two ways. As a computer science student, I know junior coding work could shrink. But the restaurant could benefit: ordering, bookings, stock levels and the books are things software could do. If I'm the one who sets that up for my family, I'd be useful in both worlds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, with care, to learn quicker and check my own work. I'd set up online bookings and a simple stock system for the restaurant over the winter break. I'd also go to the careers fair and talk to small firms, not only the big names, since they might still take juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously hopeful. It reminds me of Dad learning to use a card reader. He grumbled, and then he never wanted to go back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our waitress Aiko, who's been with us for years. She does bookings by phone, and software could take that away. I'd hate to be the one who builds the thing that replaces our waitress Aiko, so I'd want to give her a different job. She could run the front of house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your parents agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if I explain it with respect. Mum thinks of staff as family, and she'd not want anyone pushed out. So I'd say it frees people for better work, and I'd make sure it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to stay calm and look after our families first. I'd tell my parents to keep working but also to save, and I'd tell my brother to keep studying. At the temple, I'd ask my grandmother what she thinks, because she's seen big changes before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be really anxious. Two years is too short, and my degree is the kind that gets hit first. But a restaurant is hands-on, with food and people, so my parents' business should last at least until the robots come in 2031. That's the only thing keeping me upright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents the same weekend and agree what to protect. I'd stop my own spending, except food and transport. I'd go full-time at the restaurant during breaks and help move the books and bookings to simple software, so costs drop. And I'd think hard about whether to switch to something hands-on if the degree stops making sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a tight knot in my stomach, but I'd keep smiling in front of my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why smiling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Kenta's twelve and reads my face. If I look scared, he'll be scared, and he'd stop doing his homework. My job is to be the calm older sister, even if it's an act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandmother say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say hard times come and go, and a family that eats together will manage. She survived worse. I'd believe her for about a day, then I'd start worrying again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to steady ourselves. To my parents I'd say we should use the time to make the restaurant efficient, and save for the hard years. At the temple I'd say the family should be ready to support each other, since that's what we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but not alarmed. I'd graduate in 2029 or 2030, which gives me maybe a year before the main change. I'd want to build up some savings and something useful, like working systems for the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study hard and take a summer internship, ideally at a small company. I'd put in the online booking and stock system at the restaurant, and keep the books digital. I'd save 3,000 by graduation, and help Kenta with his own studies. I'd keep using AI sometimes, but I'd make sure I still understand what I hand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. Like wearing a coat for a cold winter I can see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it changes how we talk about it at home. With two years, my parents would be frightened and I'd be rushing. With five, we can have calm meetings on Sundays, and make a family plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings first. Then a decision about whether the restaurant stays as it is or if Mum and Dad would sell in time. And Kenta's education. We'd write it down, and we'd check it every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and we should prepare without fuss. I'd tell my parents that the restaurant could use some of these tools to save work and money. I'd say to friends to build skills and savings and not wait for someone else to fix things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly calm. I'd be 28, perhaps with a job and a bit of money to help the family. The thing I'd worry about is my parents getting older, because they'd be in their sixties, tired, and still running the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, get a job, and then help my parents with the restaurant: the systems, the books, and maybe cutting hours. I'd save towards helping Kenta at university. And I'd keep learning, but slowly, one new tool each year. I'd keep going to the temple, since that's where my head stays clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. Not asleep, but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your parents to retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but they'd never say it. Dad would work until he drops. So I'd quietly make the restaurant easier, with systems and a manager, so he can do fewer hours without feeling he's given up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saying something that sounds like I think they're getting old. In our family you don't say that. I'd find a way to put it as a gift, not a criticism.

Build **skills and savings** and don't wait for someone else to fix things.
think: I'd feel **fairly calm**: 28, perhaps with a job and money to help the family.
I'd worry about my **parents** getting older while still running the restaurant.

Learn **one new tool** each year, slowly.
S4.quote: I'd find a way to put it as a gift, not a criticism.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my brother would still be at school, my parents would still be running the restaurant, and I'd have no time to build a safety net. What would help is quick practical support for small businesses, honest advice to students about which jobs last, and communities that look after their own. I'd also want the government to leave families room to decide for themselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not as shy as I seem. I think the family and the community should be the first safety net, and the government the second. And that students like me work hard and ask for very little.

headlineQuote: I think the family and the community should be the first safety net, and the government the second.
portrait: Elena is an **18-year-old** computer science student whose parents run a restaurant, where she does the till and the books.
She uses AI **now and then**, with care, and wants to bring simple software to the family business.
She is **traditional** and values family, faith and respect, so she plans changes gently and as a family.
Her worry peaks at **two years**, and she hides it to be the calm older sister to her brother Kenta.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most: her brother still at school and no time to build a safety net.
whatWouldHelp: Quick practical support for **small businesses**, honest advice on which jobs last, and communities that look after their own.
